title: Men burned alive in cells, witness tells inquiry
subtitle: It is an image that will torture Silus Reuben for the rest of his life: 22-year-old Ricardo Wesley clinging to the bars of his jail cell, burning alive with no hope of escape.
article: It is an image that will torture Silus Reuben for the rest of his life: 22-year-old Ricardo Wesley clinging to the bars of his jail cell, burning alive with no hope of escape.

Reuben, a former Nishnawbe-Aski Police Service constable, testified today at a coroner's inquest into the Jan. 8, 2006 deaths of Wesley and Jamie Goodwin, 20. Both men, who had been arrested for intoxication, died in their cells when fire consumed the police detachment in Kashechewan First Nation, a fly-in community in Northern Ontario.
Police scrambled to free the men, Reuben said, describing the attempts of three other officers to unlock the cells.
The keys to the padlocked cells were not labelled, and were hanging in a nearby room when the fire broke out, the inquest heard.
"If they were labelled, I don't think it would have made a difference," said Reuben, blaming the smoke for thwarting the officers' efforts.
He said he tried in vain to find bolt-cutters to break the locks on each cell.
"I saw flames right behind Ricardo. He was screaming, shouting. He was screaming for his mother to come help him."
The inquest did not hear how a fire started inside Ricardo's cell that day, when the temperature sank to -25 C.

It is known, however, that the detention area was without heat, light, toilets and sinks. Cells were sometimes furnished with a dingy foam mattress, no more than 10 centimetres thick, and a couple of ratty blankets. They consistently smelled of urine and vomit.
The detachment had no fire alarm, no smoke detectors and no fire extinguisher.
"In the past, before this happened, we wrote letters to our union and management saying this place is an accident waiting to happen," said Reuben.
In January, 2005, officers at the detachment were ordered to stop using the cells. Detainees were instead to be driven to the detachment at Fort Albany, about 50 minutes away.
But in testimony last week, the inquest heard the winter road from Kashechewan to Fort Albany was not yet fully plowed on the day of the fire.
Much of today's testimony centred on Wesley's jacket. Reuben said he removed it when he searched Wesley at the detachment, and did not give it back.

Under cross-examination by Julian Roy, lawyer for the Wesley family, Reuben said he did not search the jacket. He also said detainees are often allowed to wear their jackets inside their cells, especially during the winter.
Part-time detachment guard Albina Nakogee also came before the inquest today. Speaking through an interpreter, Nakogee struggled to describe the events surrounding the fire.
"I saw Ricardo standing there," was all she could muster.
Roy read Nakogee excerpts from her police statement taken the day after the fire, in which she described Wesley wearing a blue coat inside his cell.
But Nakogee said she could no longer remember what Wesley was wearing.
The inquest continues tomorrow.
